claims.text: Multi-step thermomechanical treatment consisting of controlled forging and annealing can stabilize targeted phases in high-entropy alloys.
Multi-step thermomechanical treatment can refine the microstructure of high-entropy alloys.
Multi-step thermomechanical treatment can optimize the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys.
Near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys may undergo processing sequences that include casting, homogenization, deformation processing, and annealing.
A systematic sequence of multiple forging steps followed by controlled annealing is an appropriate intervention for high-entropy alloys.
Modulating forging temperature and strain rate controls the effects of multi-step thermomechanical treatment.
Elevated-temperature forging with modest strain rates and designed cooling paths can manage recrystallization kinetics.
Dynamic recrystallization and controlled phase transformations refine the microstructure.
Deformation followed by thermal exposure promotes controlled dislocation generation and annihilation.
Controlled dislocation generation and annihilation facilitate grain-boundary formation.
Deformation and subsequent thermal exposure stabilize desired phases.
The proposed mechanism increases strength without a commensurate loss of ductility.
Multi-step processing produces higher strength and ductility than as-cast or single-step thermally treated microstructures.
Single-pass processing or direct annealing leaves relatively coarse grains and less optimal mechanical properties.
Excessively high forging or annealing temperatures can cause excessive grain coarsening.
Excessively high temperatures or inadequate strain rates can produce unwanted phases and reverse the processing benefits.
Strength and ductility gains vary with alloy composition and processing parameters.
X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, tensile testing, and hardness testing can be used to evaluate phase constitution, grain size, phase distribution, and mechanical properties.
